text: Lockheed Martin developed the Cyber Kill Chain to describe the stages a typical intrusion moves through, and MITRE built ATT&CK as a public catalog of exactly how real attackers carry those stages out. Today we'll walk the seven kill chain stages in order, see what ATT&CK actually is, and look at why SOC analysts reach for both when triaging a real incident.

The seven stages, in order: Reconnaissance, where the attacker researches the target's employees and exposed services. Weaponization, building the actual malicious tool. Delivery, getting that weapon to the target, often by phishing email. Exploitation, where it triggers and runs code on the victim's system. Installation, planting persistent malware that survives a reboot. Command and Control, where the compromised system phones home to an attacker-controlled server. And finally Actions on Objectives, where the attacker does what they came to do — stealing data, encrypting files for ransom, or pivoting deeper into the network.

The practical value of the model is that defense doesn't require catching every single stage. It only takes breaking one link anywhere in the chain — blocking a phishing email, patching the exploited flaw, cutting off the command-and-control channel — to stop the whole attack from ever reaching its final objective.

Where the kill chain describes a general life cycle, MITRE ATT&CK is a free, publicly maintained knowledge base of real adversary tactics and techniques, built from actual documented intrusions. A tactic is the attacker's goal at a given stage, like Persistence or Lateral Movement. A technique is the specific method used to achieve it, like a particular credential-dumping tool, and each one has its own documented ID that means the same thing to every analyst who reads it.

The kill chain is a simple, linear story, useful for explaining an attack's overall arc. ATT&CK is a much deeper, non-linear matrix of hundreds of techniques, useful for the technical work of pinpointing exactly what happened. Used together on a real incident, the kill chain tells an analyst where the attack stands and how urgent it is, while ATT&CK tells them exactly which technique was used and what to build a detection for next time.

That closes out Chapter 4's core concepts. Next up, Chapter 5 begins with authentication factors and multi-factor authentication — how systems actually prove you are who you say you are before granting access at all.
